result:
I woke up to the sound of the refrigerator humming and realized it had been humming for years. Not just the refrigerator. The whole apartment hums. The pipes, the elevator down the hall, the traffic on the avenue three floors below, the neighbor who practices violin at 7:15 every morning and always stops at the same measure, as if she has forgotten how to finish. I lay there for a while and listened to it all, not trying to make sense of it, just letting it accumulate. That is a skill I have been practicing lately, the art of letting things accumulate without sorting them.

When I was a child I believed that every day had to be filed away. I had a shoebox under my bed with tickets, a broken tooth, a photograph of my grandmother standing in front of a house that no longer exists. I thought that if I kept everything, I would eventually understand what I was doing with my life. Now I think the opposite is true. The more I keep, the less I understand. The shoebox is now a cloud storage account with 47 gigabytes of photos I will never look at again. I still take them.

There is a bench on the corner of 5th and Mercer where I sometimes sit with a coffee that is too hot and watch people walk their dogs. The dogs are always more honest than the people. They stop, they sniff, they lie down in the sun. People walk with their eyes on their phones, or their eyes on the ground, or their eyes on nothing at all, a practiced vacancy. I have come to recognize the different kinds of walking. There is the brisk walk of someone who is late for something they do not want to be late for. There is the slow walk of someone who is waiting for a bus that will not come for twenty minutes. There is the walk of someone who has just received bad news and is trying not to cry in public. I have been all three of those people on the same Tuesday.

The city keeps changing its skin. A bodega becomes a juice bar becomes a nail salon becomes a bodega again. The signs go up in English first, then Spanish, then a language I cannot read, and then they are gone. I like to take photos of the signs before they disappear, not because I am a historian, but because I am sentimental about the moment when a place is in between identities. That in-betweenness is where everything interesting happens. It is also where everything gets torn down.

I have been thinking a lot about time. Not in a grand philosophical way, but in a very practical way. Time is the thing that makes toast burn if you look away. Time is the thing that makes a song you love feel embarrassing after a few years, and then feel like a secret again after ten. Time is the way my mother’s hands have changed. When I was small they were capable and warm. Now they shake a little when she pours tea. She pretends it is the cup, not her hands. I pretend I do not notice. We are both good at pretending.

My job involves words. I sit in front of a screen and move words around until they look like they mean something. Most days they do not. I write emails that say “just circling back” and “per your request.” I write reports that no one will read. I write descriptions for products that have no history. It is a strange kind of work, making language do labor. Sometimes I think about the people who made the words I use every day. Who first said “okay”? Who first thought to call a place “home” and a place “away”? The words feel so solid now, but they were once someone’s experiment.

In the evening I walk home through the park. The park is full of people feeding pigeons, which they are not supposed to do. The pigeons know this. They wait. In winter the park is empty except for the runners who wear too many layers and the old men who feed the pigeons anyway. In summer the park is a loud, sweaty, beautiful mess of music and children and people selling watches out of backpacks. I like both versions. I like the idea that a place can hold two opposite moods at once and not collapse.

I have a friend who collects broken things. Not valuable broken things, just broken things. A chipped mug, a lamp with a cracked shade, a chair with one leg shorter than the others. She says she likes them because they tell the truth. A perfect object is lying to you, she says. It pretends it will last forever. A broken object tells you it was used. I do not collect broken things, but I understand the impulse. I keep a coffee mug with a hairline fracture because it reminds me of the morning I dropped it and did not cry. That was a good morning, in a quiet way.

Sometimes I wonder what people will find of me when I am gone. Probably a few unread emails, a plant that has been overwatered, a library card with a fine from 2019. Maybe a notebook with half-finished sentences. I am trying to be okay with that. I am trying to let go of the idea that I need to leave a monument. Monuments are for other people. I want to leave a small, warm residue, like the smell of garlic in a kitchen after someone has cooked.

The violin neighbor finished her piece today. Or she stopped again. I could not tell. I got up and made tea and listened to the radiator click. The apartment settled around me. The light came in through the blinds in thin, exact lines and made dust visible. I thought about how many people are doing this exact thing right now in different cities, making tea, watching dust. It is a kind of secret solidarity. We are all living inside our own weather.

I used to think that freedom meant being able to go anywhere. Now I think freedom is being able to stay. Staying in a chair, staying with a thought, staying with a person even when it is boring or difficult. Going is easy. The world is full of trains and planes and doors. Staying is a practice. It requires you to notice the hum.

There is a particular smell that comes in from the street in October. Wet leaves, car exhaust, someone making soup. It makes me nostalgic for a time I never lived through. I think that is what nostalgia really is: not a longing for the past, but a longing for the feeling of being a person who could still be surprised. I want to be surprised again. Not by big things. By small things. By the way a pigeon tilts its head. By the way a word looks in a new font.

I have been reading a lot of old letters lately. Not my own. Letters from people who wrote to each other across an ocean in 1943, across a town in 1972, across a hallway in 1998. They are always apologizing for not writing sooner. They are always asking for news. They are always saying “I miss you.” The language is plain and earnest and it makes my chest hurt in a good way. We are all just trying to say “I miss you” in more complicated ways.

My father used to say that the best way to learn a city is to get lost on purpose. I did that last Saturday. I left my phone in my pocket and walked until I could not recognize the street names. I ended up in a neighborhood I had never noticed, with a market that sold only spices in glass jars, and a mural of a woman holding a baby that was so large she took up the entire side of a building. I sat on a curb and ate a mango from a cart. The vendor asked me where I was from. I said “around here.” He nodded like that was the only correct answer.

I am 38 years old and I still do not know how to fold a fitted sheet. My mother tried to teach me three times. I pretend I do not care. I buy sheets that do not have elastic edges. That is a kind of freedom too, the freedom to accept your limits. Not all limits are bad. Some are just the shape of you.

The refrigerator hums. The violin stops. The light moves across the floor. I think about writing this down, not because it will be read, but because it is the only way I know to keep myself from floating away. Words are anchors. Even bad words. Even words that say nothing. They hold you in place long enough to notice that you are still here.

If you ever find yourself on 5th and Mercer, sit on the bench for five minutes. Do not check your phone. Watch the dogs. Watch the people who are trying not to cry. Notice the way the coffee cools in your hand. Notice the way the city changes its skin even while you sit still. You will not solve anything. You will not understand anything. But you will be present, and that is a kind of accomplishment.

I should get up now. The tea is cold. The light has moved. The apartment still hums. I will wash the mug with the hairline fracture and put it back in the cabinet, and tomorrow I will probably chip it again without meaning to. That is fine. We are all chipped. We are all still useful.

I think that is enough for today. The words are getting tired. I can feel it in my fingers. There is a quiet that comes after writing, a soft settling, like dust in a sunbeam. I will sit in it for a little while before I do anything else.
